The most popular measurement system within the scientific community is the **metric system**. 

We determine how much space an object occupies by measuring its **volume**. We use **volume units** to specify an object's volume. 

A common metric unit of volume is the **liter,** which we denote using the symbol "$\textrm{L}$." We can use **measuring jugs** like the ones below to measure the volume of a liquid.

![](images/fa/fa15e2d9b446412876732435aa06b8117fbb4903ab179e4cc64c50da4868fee7.png)

We use **milliliters** to measure smaller volumes. The symbol for milliliters is "$\textrm{mL}.$" The prefix $\textrm m$ stands for **milli,** which means $\dfrac{1}{1\,000}.$ Therefore, $1\,\textrm{mL}$ equals $\dfrac{1}{1\,000}\,\textrm L.$

Notice that if we add $1\,\textrm{mL}$ to itself $1\,000$ times, we get exactly $1\,\textrm{L}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{1\,000\text{ times}}{\overset{⏞}{1\,\text{mL}+1\,\text{mL}+⋯+1\,\text{mL}}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L}+\frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L}+⋯+\frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ 1\,000\times \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ \frac{1\,000\times 1}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ \frac{1\,000}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ 1\,\text{L}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $1\,000\,\textrm{mL}$ equals $1\,\textrm{L},$ as stated in the diagram." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199505 :tutorial/content "Another way to measure volume is to use **customary units.** The most common customary units for volume are **fluid ounce**, **cup**, **pint**, and **gallon**.

A table showing the customary units of volume is given below.

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gallon | $\textrm{gal}$ | $1\,\textrm{gal} = 8\,\textrm{pints}$ |
| Pint | $\textrm{pt}$ | $1\,\textrm{pt} = 2\,\textrm{cups}$ |
| Cup | $-$ | $1\,\textrm{cup} = 8\,\textrm{fl oz}$ |
| Fluid ounce | $\textrm{fl oz}$ | $-$ |

Note that "gallons" is the largest volume unit, and "fluid ounces" is the smallest. 

Customary units are not standard in the scientific community. However, they are commonly used in the United States and other countries." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198503 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

The most popular measurement system within the scientific community is the **metric system**. 

We determine how much space an object occupies by measuring its **volume**. We use **volume units** to specify an object's volume. 

A common metric unit of volume is the **liter,** which we denote using the symbol "$\textrm{L}$." We can use **measuring jugs** like the ones below to measure the volume of a liquid.

![](images/fa/fa15e2d9b446412876732435aa06b8117fbb4903ab179e4cc64c50da4868fee7.png)

We use **milliliters** to measure smaller volumes. The symbol for milliliters is "$\textrm{mL}.$" The prefix $\textrm m$ stands for **milli,** which means $\dfrac{1}{1\,000}.$ Therefore, $1\,\textrm{mL}$ equals $\dfrac{1}{1\,000}\,\textrm L.$

Notice that if we add $1\,\textrm{mL}$ to itself $1\,000$ times, we get exactly $1\,\textrm{L}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{1\,000\text{ times}}{\overset{⏞}{1\,\text{mL}+1\,\text{mL}+⋯+1\,\text{mL}}} & = \\ \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L}+\frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L}+⋯+\frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ 1\,000\times \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ \frac{1\,000\times 1}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ \frac{1\,000}{1\,000}\,\text{L} & = \\ 1\,\text{L}\end{aligned}
$$

The most popular measurement system within the scientific community is the **metric system**.

We determine how much space an object occupies by measuring its **volume**. We use **volume units** to specify an object's volume.

A common metric unit of volume is the **liter,** which we denote using the symbol "$\textrm{L}$." We can use **measuring jugs** like the ones below to measure the volume of a liquid.

![](images/fa/fa15e2d9b446412876732435aa06b8117fbb4903ab179e4cc64c50da4868fee7.png)

We use **milliliters** to measure smaller volumes. The symbol for milliliters is "$\textrm{mL}$." The prefix $\textrm m$ stands for **milli,** which means

$$
\dfrac{1}{1\,000}
$$

Therefore, $1\,\textrm{mL}$ equals

$$
\dfrac{1}{1\,000}\,\textrm L
$$

Notice that if we add $1\,\textrm{mL}$ to itself $1\,000$ times, we get exactly $1\,\textrm{L}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
1mL + 1mL + ⋯ + 1mL^(⏞)^(1000times) &=  \\
\frac{1}{1000}L + \frac{1}{1000}L + ⋯ + \frac{1}{1000}L &=  \\
1000 \cdot \frac{1}{1000}L &=  \\
\frac{1000 \cdot 1}{1000}L &=  \\
\frac{1000}{1000}L &=  \\
&= 1L
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $1\,000\,\textrm{mL}$ equals $1\,\textrm{L}$, as stated in the diagram." :tutorial/id #uuid "134c077c-df22-5aea-bfa9-f7c4716a73cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7791 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199356 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198424 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198066 :question/id #uuid "c0546e5d-93b8-5ccd-9833-c5d1cfc1533a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12512"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1b8161e6-678c-5fb6-b1bd-3e3d78913495" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198667} {:db/id 17592186198668}] :knowledge-point/title "Metric Units of Volume"} :step/id #uuid "fb4a9756-596a-54cc-983a-27b78164ef81" :step/math-academy-id 45092 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199379}} {:db/id 17592186199379 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199505 :tutorial/content "Another way to measure volume is to use **customary units.** The most common customary units for volume are **fluid ounce**, **cup**, **pint**, and **gallon**.

A table showing the customary units of volume is given below.

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Gallon | $\textrm{gal}$ | $1\,\textrm{gal} = 8\,\textrm{pints}$ |
| Pint | $\textrm{pt}$ | $1\,\textrm{pt} = 2\,\textrm{cups}$ |
| Cup | $-$ | $1\,\textrm{cup} = 8\,\textrm{fl oz}$ |
| Fluid ounce | $\textrm{fl oz}$ | $-$ |

Note that "gallons" is the largest volume unit, and "fluid ounces" is the smallest.

Customary units are not standard in the scientific community. We use **milliliters** to measure smaller volumes. The symbol for milliliters is "$\textrm{mL}$." The prefix $\textrm m$ stands for **milli,** which means

$$
\dfrac{1}{1\,000}
$$

Therefore, $1\,\textrm{mL}$ equals

$$
\dfrac{1}{1\,000}\,\textrm L
$$

\frac{1000 \cdot 1}{1000}L &=  \\

&= 1L
\end{aligned}
$$
